title-group.article-title: Short- and long-term prognostic analysis of supraclavicular oblique incision versus traditional low-collar incision in thyroidectomy

abstract.p: Thyroidectomy is the primary treatment for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and the type of incision has a significant impact on the short- and long-term recovery of patients. This retrospective study included data from 280 patients with PTC who underwent thyroidectomy. Patients were divided into 2 groups according to incision type: traditional low-collar incision thyroidectomy (TLCIT); and supraclavicular oblique incision thyroidectomy (SOIT). Demographic characteristics, clinical features, and postoperative complications were compared between the 2 groups. Generalized estimating equations were used to analyze the effects of the 2 incision types on short-term (postoperative pain, wound swelling, heat sensation, and neck discomfort) and long-term (quality of life, scar score, anxiety, and depression scores) indicators. In terms of short-term recovery, SOIT significantly reduced postoperative pain, wound swelling, sensation of heat, and neck discomfort. Interaction analysis revealed that SOIT had a significant effect on reducing postoperative pain 1 week after surgery and on reducing heat sensation and neck discomfort 1 month after surgery. In terms of long-term effects, SOIT significantly improved Short-Form-36 and EQ-5D quality of life scores, reduced scar scores, and decreased anxiety and depression scores. Interaction analysis further indicated that SOIT significantly reduced scar scores at 3 and 6 months postoperatively, and significantly reduced anxiety scores at 6 months postoperatively. Compared with the traditional low-collar incision, the supraclavicular oblique incision yielded better short- and long-term prognoses in thyroidectomies for patients diagnosed with PTC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, thyroid cancer has become one of the fastest-growing malignant tumors in terms of incidence. Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common type, accounting for approximately 60%–70% of all cases [1, 2]. With advances in diagnostic technologies and improvements in public health awareness, the detection rate of PTC has been continuously increasing and has become a significant threat to public health [3, 4]. PTC grows slowly and, when detected and treated at an early stage, has a favorable prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate exceeding 90%. Currently, the primary treatments for PTC include surgical resection, radioactive iodine therapy, and thyroid-stimulating hormone suppression therapy, among which surgical resection is the first-line treatment [5, 6]. The benefits of thyroidectomy are based on its ability to effectively remove cancerous tissue, reduce the risk for metastasis and recurrence, and create favorable conditions for subsequent radioactive iodine therapy [7]. However, different types of surgical incisions have varying effects on short- and long-term postoperative recovery.

Traditional low-collar incision thyroidectomy (TLCIT), a classic surgical method, provides a larger incision area and good surgical field exposure, which helps surgeons perform more precise maneuvers to ensure complete tumor removal [8]. However, TLCIT is also associated with a higher risk for postoperative complications, including temporary hypoparathyroidism, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, postoperative pain, and hoarseness, all of which can affect recovery rate and quality of life (QoL). In addition, TLCIT may affect the appearance of scars on the neck, creating a psychological burden on some patients. Therefore, determining an incision method that can reduce complications, improve QoL, and enhance aesthetic outcomes has become a focal point of clinical attention.

In recent years, supraclavicular oblique incision thyroidectomy (SOIT) has been gradually applied to thyroidectomy [9]. Compared with TLCIT, SOIT has a more concealed location, shorter incision length, and less impact on neck appearance, which are considered to have advantages in reducing postoperative pain and complications and improving patient satisfaction. However, comparative studies of the clinical applications of SOIT and TLCIT are relatively novel. Current research has only conducted simple differential analyses, lacking a more in-depth analysis of changes over time, and have not included psychological assessment(s), which is not sufficiently comprehensive [10, 11].

This study aimed to provide systematic and comprehensive evidence supporting the application of SOIT or TLCIT in surgery for PTC, offering a scientific basis for incision selection. Our goal was to optimize postoperative recovery and improve QoL and psychological health, thereby providing patients diagnosed with PTC a better postoperative experience and long-term health benefits.

sec.title: Patient selection
sec.p: This retrospective cohort study collected data from patients diagnosed with PTC who underwent thyroidectomy at the authors’ hospital between January 2020 and December 2023. Inclusion criteria were as follows: no history of neck surgery or head and neck radiotherapy; unilateral thyroid nodule with a diameter ≤2 cm, initially suspected as thyroid cancer based on preoperative ultrasound, computed tomography, or fine-needle aspiration biopsy, with no signs of extrathyroidal (e.g., trachea, esophagus, carotid artery, or mediastinum) invasion or metastasis; age between 18 and 75 years; and complete preoperative assessment, intraoperative records, and postoperative follow-up data. The exclusion criteria were as follows: history of thyroid cancer surgery; other malignant tumors; severe cardiopulmonary dysfunction or other contraindications for surgery; and loss to follow-up or incomplete data. This study was approved by the hospital ethics committee, and informed written consent was obtained from all patients.

sec.title: Collection of demographic and clinical characteristics
sec.p: Basic demographic data were collected, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking, and alcohol consumption habits, as well as preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative clinical characteristics, including tumor size, incision length, surgery time, intraoperative blood loss, drainage volume, and drainage duration. Additionally, postoperative complications, such as temporary hypoparathyroidism and transient recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, were recorded.

sec.title: Surgical procedure
sec.p: The main surgical steps included preoperative preparation and incision marking, anesthesia and position adjustment, incision opening and flap dissection, exposure of the thyroid gland, nerve and parathyroid gland protection, thyroidectomy, lymph node dissection, surgical area examination and drainage, and incision closure. The primary difference between the supraclavicular oblique incision (SOI) and traditional low-collar incision (TLCI) lies in their location and approach. The SOI was positioned 1–2 cm above the clavicle, following a slanted line along the clavicle, resulting in a smaller and more concealed incision. The TLCI is located in the lower neck, usually 5–7 cm above the sternal notch, and is made horizontally along the natural skin crease. The incision is relatively long. SOI involves direct dissection of the muscle layers, carefully protecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid glands and enabling thyroidectomy to be completed with minimal traction on the muscles and nerves. In contrast, TLCI accesses the midline of the neck (cervical linea alba) by separating the infrahyoid muscles along the midline without cutting the muscle, providing greater exposure while minimizing muscle layer injury.

All surgical procedures were performed by a single surgical team with more than 10 years’ experience in thyroid surgery and were proficient in both TLCIT and SOIT. To minimize the potential influence of surgeon variability on the outcomes, the 3 surgeons reached a pre-study consensus regarding the operative steps and key intraoperative procedures to ensure consistent execution of surgical techniques.

sec.title: Evaluation of short-term clinical recovery indicators
sec.p: Short-term clinical recovery indicators included postoperative pain, wound swelling, hoarseness, and neck discomfort. On postoperative days 1, 3, and 7, and at 1 month, wound swelling (classified as no swelling, mild redness without exudate, exudate or mild infection, and significant redness or infection), hoarseness (evaluated using the Voice Handicap Index [VHI]-10 scale), and neck discomfort levels were recorded based on patient complaints and physician assessments. Postoperative pain was assessed using a visual analog scale on postoperative days 1, 3, and 7. A generalized estimating equation (GEE) model was used to analyze the interaction between the incision type and recovery time to evaluate the effects of the 2 incisions on these indicators during postoperative recovery. Neck discomfort was classified into 4 levels: no sensory abnormality (completely normal, no discomfort); mild sensory abnormality (slight discomfort without affecting daily life); moderate sensory abnormality (significant discomfort, occasionally affecting daily life); and severe sensory abnormality (persistent discomfort, significantly affecting daily activities).

sec.title: Evaluation of long-term QoL and satisfaction
sec.p: To evaluate the long-term impact of the 2 incision types on patient QoL and satisfaction, follow-up assessments were performed at 1 week, and 1, 3, and 6 months postoperatively. The main assessment tools included the following: Short-Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36) to evaluate overall QoL; EQ-5D scale to assess health status and QoL; Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale (POSAS) to evaluate the appearance of scars and patient satisfaction with scars; and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scales (HADS–A and HADS–D) to assess psychological health, including anxiety and depression. All scales were completed by the patients under the guidance of trained medical staff.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All data were analyzed using R (R Core Team; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Continuous variables are expressed as median (minimum–maximum) and were compared between groups using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables are expressed as frequency and percentage, and were compared using the chi-squared test. Multivariate logistic regression was used to analyze risk factors for complications, and the GEE [12] was applied to assess the interaction effects of incision type and time on short-term recovery and long-term QoL.

sec.title: Differences in demographic and clinical characteristics
sec.p: The median age of all patients was 44 years (range, 25–66 years), with males and females accounting for 22.5% and 77.5%, respectively. Among all patients, the median BMI was 24.07 kg/m2 (range, 17.71–31.54 kg/m2), 8.21% were smokers, and 9.64% consumed alcohol. The median tumor size was 1.56 cm (range, 0.50–2.50 cm). The proportion of patients with unifocal tumors was 81.79%, whereas those with multifocal tumors accounted for 18.21%. The median incision length for all patients was 5.00 cm (range, 3.64–6.54 cm), and the incision length in the SOIT group was significantly smaller than that in the TLCIT group. The median duration of surgery for all patients was 69.29 min (range, 54.02–86.48 min), and surgery duration for the SOIT group was significantly lower than that for the TLCIT group. Intraoperative blood loss of all patients was 38.40 mL (range 23.74–56.41 mL), with blood loss in the SOIT group significantly lower than that in the TLCIT group. The median drainage volume of all patients was 50.21 mL (range 33.80–66.53 mL), and the postoperative drainage volume of the SOIT group was significantly lower than that of the TLCIT group. The median drainage duration for all patients was 4 days (range, 3–4.5 days), and drainage duration in the SOIT group was significantly lower than that in the TLCIT group. The median number of dissected central lymph nodes for all patients was 7 (range, 5–9) (Table 1).

sec.title: Analysis of differences in postoperative complications between the SOIT and TLCIT groups
sec.p: Among all patients, complications were distributed as follows: temporary hypoparathyroidism (2.86% [n = 8]); temporary recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (1.79% [n = 5]); bleeding or hematoma (1.07% [n = 3]); and infection (0.71% [n = 2]). The incidence of complications was lower in the SOIT group than that in the TLCIT group, although the difference was not significant (Table 2).

caption.title: Multivariate logistic regression analysis of risk factors influencing the occurrence of complications

sec.title: Analysis of short-term clinical recovery indicators
sec.p: Compared with TLCIT, SOIT significantly reduced postoperative pain. The interaction between surgical incision and time had a significant impact on pain, and over time (especially 1 week after surgery), the pain level decreased by 71.8% (p < 0.05). In terms of postoperative wound swelling, SOIT reduced the degree of wound redness and infection. However, the interaction effect with time was not significant. SOIT also played a significant role in reducing hoarseness and, over time, the p-value became more significant. One month postoperatively, the degree of hoarseness had decreased by 71.3%. SOIT also significantly reduced neck discomfort, with a notable interaction effect at 1 month post-surgery, resulting in a 45.8% reduction in neck discomfort (Table 3).

sec.title: Analysis of long-term QoL and satisfaction indicators
sec.p: SOIT significantly improved SF-36 and EQ-5D scores; however, the interaction effect with time was not significant. In terms of scar score, SOIT significantly reduced scar scores, and the effect became more significant over time. At 3 months, the scar score decreased by 47.8% and, at 6 months, the scar score decreased by 87.8%. SOIT also significantly reduced patient anxiety and depression scores. The interaction effect of time was significant for anxiety scores. Six months after surgery, anxiety scores significantly reduced by 15.9%, while the interaction effect with time on depression scores was not significant (Table 4).

sec.title: Trends in short- and long-term recovery indicators over time
sec.p: Regarding short-term indicators, with an increase in postoperative recovery time, the pain level, wound swelling degree, hoarseness, and neck discomfort degree all significantly decreased. Moreover, the SOIT group exhibited a higher rate of pain decrease, hoarseness, and degree of neck discomfort relief degree at T2–T3 (1 week to 1 month after surgery) than the TLCIT group (Fig. 1A–D). In the long-term indicators, with an increase in postoperative recovery time, QoL, scar aesthetics, anxiety, and significantly improved depression levels. However, compared with the TLCIT group, the SOIT group exhibited greater improvement and a more significant effect at 6 months after surgery (Fig. 2A–E).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study compared the short- and long-term clinical outcomes of SOIT and TLCIT. The results demonstrated that SOIT significantly outperformed TLCIT in improving short-term postoperative outcomes including pain levels, wound swelling, hoarseness, and neck discomfort. Additionally, SOIT yielded superior long-term benefits in terms of QoL, scar appearance, and reduction in anxiety and depression.

SOIT has multiple advantages, including a shorter incision length, shorter surgical duration, lower intraoperative bleeding, and lower postoperative drainage volume and time. This is due to the fact that SOIT does not need to cross the entire neck—as in TLCIT—but directly enters the thyroid gland through natural anatomical gaps, resulting in smaller incisions. The SOIT procedure is simple, reduces tissue separation time, and the incision is closer to the thyroid gland, which is beneficial for faster search and identification. Due to the lack of large-scale separation of the latissimus and anterior cervical muscle groups, suturing speed was also faster, resulting in a shorter surgical duration. SOIT avoids densely populated areas such as the anterior jugular vein during surgery and has high electrocoagulation efficiency, making it easier to stop bleeding, resulting in less intraoperative bleeding. Due to the minimal trauma and lymphatic vessel damage caused by SOIT, as well as the lower position of the incision during postoperative drainage, which facilitates fluid drainage, the drainage volume and time were relatively small and short.

The SOIT incision yields significant advantages in terms of postoperative pain, wound swelling, hoarseness, and neck discomfort, mainly due to its smaller incision trauma and concealed location. SOIT avoids the traditional low neck incision that requires cutting the cervical linea alba and separating the anterior cervical muscles, preserving relatively intact muscle tissue and reducing nerve damage. Therefore, the incidence of muscle spasms, inflammatory reactions after surgery, and degree of pain are low. Avoiding separation of the anterior cervical muscles and avoiding dense lymphatic areas can also reduce traumatic edema [13]. Because SOIT directly reaches the lower pole of the thyroid gland, nerves can be exposed without excessive flipping of the thyroid gland and then operated on from bottom to top, reducing tension on the gland and lowering the tension of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. If the lesion is located below the thyroid gland, there is no need to operate upward to avoid damage to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve as much as possible. Additionally, due to the shorter operative duration of SOIT, the risk for endotracheal tube cuff pressure is reduced, thereby reducing throat damage, hoarseness, and neck discomfort [14].

Due to the reduction in postoperative pain, wound swelling, and other discomforts, SOIT enables patients to recover faster from daily activities, such as eating and speaking, resulting in a significant improvement in long-term QoL. The SOIT is located in a concealed position in the supraclavicular fossa, which can be covered by clothing and is less likely to be noticed in daily life. The risk for scar hyperplasia caused by small incisions is also lower, resulting in a significant improvement in scar aesthetics. Informing patients of the advantages of SOIT before surgery reduces their fear and anxiety, and rapid recovery after surgery enhances their confidence, reduces concerns about complications, and lowers their levels of anxiety and depression.

Surgical resection is the preferred method for treating PTC and the type of incision has a significant impact on postoperative recovery, risk for complications, and QoL [15-17]. Although SOIT is not strictly classified as a minimally invasive surgery, the shorter incision length and reduced tissue trauma partially embody the principles of minimally invasive techniques. It reduces postoperative pain, lowers the incidence of complications, and enhances aesthetic outcomes and patient satisfaction [18-20]. With advances in minimally invasive technologies, future studies should explore the use of minimally invasive techniques, such as endoscopic or robot-assisted surgeries, to minimize tissue damage and optimize surgical outcomes.

In our study, the incidences of temporary hypoparathyroidism and temporary recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in the TLCIT group were 3.3% and 2.2%, respectively. The respective incidences in the SOIT group were lower than those in the TLCIT group; however, the difference was not statistically significant. These rates are within the range reported in the literature. A meta-analysis reported that the incidence of temporary hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy ranges from 1% to 58% [21]. Another study reported that the incidence of temporary recurrent laryngeal nerve injury ranges from 1.5% to 14% [22]. This indicates that the surgical safety of both the TLCIT and SOIT incision approaches in our study was generally good, with complication rates within an acceptable range.

In this study, the SF-36, EQ-5D, POSAS, and HADS were selected as postoperative QoL assessment tools, primarily based on their comprehensiveness and complementarity. The SF-36 and EQ-5D, which are internationally recognized generic QoL instruments, can comprehensively reflect patient physical function, psychological status, social function, and overall health. The HADS focuses on anxiety and depression, complementing the psychological dimensions of the SF-36 and EQ-5D, and enabling a thorough assessment of postoperative psychological recovery. The POSAS provides an objective evaluation of the visual appearance of scars and patients’ subjective perceptions, which are particularly important for thyroid surgery because neck scars may impact both QoL and psychological well-being. Other scales, such as the Thyroid Cancer-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (i.e., “THYCA-QoL”), a thyroid cancer–specific QoL questionnaire that is more precise in assessing thyroid-related functional impairments and postoperative symptoms, cover relatively limited dimensions of overall health and social functioning. The optimal approach is to combine THYCA-QoL with SF-36, EQ-5D, POSAS, and HADS, thereby fully addressing all dimensions of recovery in patients with thyroid cancer and providing a more scientific and comprehensive basis for postoperative rehabilitation management.

In this study, we applied a GEE model to evaluate the interaction between the incision type and postoperative recovery time, thereby revealing the dynamic patterns of recovery at different stages. The results revealed that SOIT yielded the most significant improvement in hoarseness and neck discomfort 1 month after surgery, while demonstrating greater effects on scar satisfaction and anxiety reduction at 3 and 6 months postoperatively. These findings highlight the stage-specific priorities for postoperative care, an aspect rarely addressed in previous studies. Moreover, the indicators included in our investigation were more comprehensive than those used in previous studies. In addition to traditional short-term clinical recovery indicators (such as pain, wound swelling, hoarseness, and neck discomfort), we incorporated assessments of QoL, anxiety, and depression to provide a multidimensional evaluation that covered both the physiological and psychological aspects of recovery.

This was a retrospective study; as such, it was susceptible to selection bias. Several measures were implemented during the research process to minimize this bias. First, all cases included in this study were consecutively collected from the same hospital within a clearly defined period. The inclusion and exclusion of cases were based entirely on objective criteria rather than researcher preferences or patient characteristics, thereby reducing the likelihood of selection bias. In addition, to further control for potential confounding factors, we used a GEE model in the analysis to adjust for relevant covariates, such as tumor size, enabling a more accurate assessment of the independent impact of incision type on both short- and long-term outcomes.

This study had some limitations, the first of which was its retrospective design, which may have introduced a degree of selection bias. In addition, the research scale was small and there were many subjective indicators. Future research should expand the sample size, conduct multicenter prospective studies, and combine multiple objective physiological and biochemical indicators to support the conclusions of this study. Although the surgical procedures were standardized, and a uniform operative protocol was strictly followed, the fact that multiple surgeons performed the operations made it difficult to completely eliminate the potential influence of inter-surgeon variability on specified outcomes. In future studies, a single-surgeon design or technical assistance could be adopted to further reduce this potential interference.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: As illustrated in the Graphical Abstract, the results of the present study indicate that SOIT has better short- and long-term prognostic effects than TLCIT in patients diagnosed with PTC. In clinical practice, SOIT can be used to provide better postoperative experiences and life satisfaction in patients undergoing surgery for PTC.

caption.title: 280 patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma who underwent thyroidectomy have been chosen. According to different incision types, the patients were divided into the traditional low-collar incision thyroidectomy group (TLCIT) and the supraclavicular oblique incision thyroidectomy group (SOIT). Compared with the traditional low-collar incision, the supraclavicular oblique incision shows better short-term and long-term prognosis in thyroidectomy for patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma.
